title: Two pointers
summary: Walk two indices in coordinated order to shrink work from quadratic to linear.

parts.rule: Place two indices on a sequence and move them according to a rule that never needs to reconsider discarded positions. Classic shapes: opposite ends moving inward on a sorted array, and a slow/fast pair on a linked list or for in-place filtering. Aim for O(n) time after any required sort.
parts.why: Nested loops over pairs are the default wrong answer on sorted arrays and palindrome checks. Two pointers reclaim linear time by using order. Bugs are moving the wrong pointer, forgetting the sort prerequisite, or using two pointers on unsorted data where order does not help.
parts.example: Pair sum to 9 on sorted [1, 2, 4, 4, 7, 11]. Left=0 (1), right=5 (11). Sum 12 too big → right--. Now right=4 (7), sum 8 too small → left++. Left=1 (2), sum 9 → found pair (2,7). Each step moves one pointer; indices never reverse. For a palindrome check on "abba": left=0, right=3 compare equal; left=1, right=2 compare equal; done. For linked-list cycle: slow and fast start at head; fast moves two steps, slow one; meeting means a cycle. On 1→2→3→4→2… they meet inside the loop after a few advances.
parts.use: Use opposite-end pointers on sorted arrays for two-sum variants and container-with-water shapes. Use slow/fast for cycles and middle-of-list. Use read/write pointers to compact a list in place after a predicate filter.
parts.refuse: Refuse two pointers as a substitute for a hash map on unsorted two-sum when you are not allowed to sort. Refuse moving both pointers every iteration without an invariant. Refuse assuming sorted order the prompt did not give. Refuse slow/fast on structures that are not singly linked in the way the proof needs.

body:
Rule. Place two indices on a sequence and move them according to a rule that never needs to reconsider discarded positions. Classic shapes: opposite ends moving inward on a sorted array, and a slow/fast pair on a linked list or for in-place filtering. Aim for O(n) time after any required sort.

Why it matters. Nested loops over pairs are the default wrong answer on sorted arrays and palindrome checks. Two pointers reclaim linear time by using order. Bugs are moving the wrong pointer, forgetting the sort prerequisite, or using two pointers on unsorted data where order does not help.

Worked example. Pair sum to 9 on sorted [1, 2, 4, 4, 7, 11]. Left=0 (1), right=5 (11). Sum 12 too big → right--. Now right=4 (7), sum 8 too small → left++. Left=1 (2), sum 9 → found pair (2,7). Each step moves one pointer; indices never reverse. For a palindrome check on "abba": left=0, right=3 compare equal; left=1, right=2 compare equal; done. For linked-list cycle: slow and fast start at head; fast moves two steps, slow one; meeting means a cycle. On 1→2→3→4→2… they meet inside the loop after a few advances.

When to use. Use opposite-end pointers on sorted arrays for two-sum variants and container-with-water shapes. Use slow/fast for cycles and middle-of-list. Use read/write pointers to compact a list in place after a predicate filter.

When to refuse. Refuse two pointers as a substitute for a hash map on unsorted two-sum when you are not allowed to sort. Refuse moving both pointers every iteration without an invariant. Refuse assuming sorted order the prompt did not give. Refuse slow/fast on structures that are not singly linked in the way the proof needs.
